prompt: What is the shape of a carbocation around its positively charged carbon?

choices.text: Planar, with the three groups at the corners of a triangle
Tetrahedral, with the groups 109.5° apart like an sp3 carbon
choices.why: The trivalent carbon is sp2-hybridized, so its three groups lie in a plane, 120° apart.

choices.text: Linear, with the substituents arranged 180° apart
choices.why: There are three substituents, not two, and they are 120° apart in a plane.

choices.text: Pyramidal, with a lone pair above the three groups
choices.why: The positive carbon has no lone pair; its p orbital is empty, and the three groups are planar.

explanation: Experimental evidence shows that carbocations are planar. The trivalent carbon is sp2-hybridized, and its three substituents point toward the corners of an equilateral triangle, with a vacant p orbital perpendicular to that plane.

prompt: How is the positively charged carbon of a carbocation hybridized?

choices.text: sp2
sp3
choices.why: An sp3 carbon has four groups in a tetrahedral arrangement. The carbocation carbon has three, in a plane.

choices.text: sp
choices.why: An sp carbon is linear with two groups. The carbocation carbon is planar with three.

choices.text: It is unhybridized
choices.why: The three σ bonds use sp2 hybrid orbitals; only the empty p orbital is left unhybridized.

explanation: The trivalent carbon of a carbocation is sp2-hybridized. Its three sp2 orbitals form σ bonds in a plane at 120°, and the remaining p orbital, perpendicular to the plane, is empty.

prompt: What is the angle between the bonds to the positively charged carbon of a carbocation, in degrees?
explanation: The three substituents point toward the corners of an equilateral triangle, so the bond angles are 120° (Figure 7.9.1).

prompt: What occupies the p orbital of a carbocation's positively charged carbon?

choices.text: Nothing; it is vacant
A lone pair of electrons
choices.why: The positive carbon has only six valence electrons, all used in its three σ bonds; none are left for a lone pair.

choices.text: A single unpaired electron
choices.why: An unpaired electron would make it a radical. In a carbocation the p orbital is empty.

choices.text: A π bond to a neighboring carbon
choices.why: The carbocation carbon has only its three σ bonds. Its p orbital is unoccupied.

explanation: Because there are only six valence electrons on the carbon and all six are used in the three σ bonds, the p orbital extending above and below the plane is unoccupied.

prompt: How many valence electrons does the positively charged carbon of a carbocation have?
explanation: The carbocation carbon has six valence electrons, all used in its three σ bonds (two electrons each). Its p orbital is empty.

prompt: What is the order of carbocation stability, most stable first?

choices.text: Tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl
Methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary
choices.why: That's reversed. Stability increases with substitution.

choices.text: Secondary > tertiary > primary > methyl
choices.why: Tertiary carbocations, with three alkyl groups, are the most stable.

choices.text: Primary > secondary > tertiary > methyl
choices.why: Stability increases steadily with the number of alkyl groups on the positive carbon.

explanation: Thermodynamic measurements show that carbocation stability increases with increasing substitution: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.

prompt: How is the carbocation (CH3)2CHCH+CH3 classified?

choices.text: Secondary
Primary
choices.why: A primary carbocation has one alkyl group on the positive carbon. Here the positive carbon carries two: CH3 and CH(CH3)2.

choices.text: Tertiary
choices.why: The CH carbon carrying two methyls is bonded to three carbons, but it isn't the positive one. The positive carbon has two alkyl groups.

choices.text: Methyl
choices.why: A methyl cation is CH3+, with no alkyl groups at all.

explanation: The positively charged carbon is bonded to a CH3 group, a CH(CH3)2 group, and one hydrogen: two alkyl substituents. That makes it a secondary carbocation (Exercise 7.9.2).

prompt: Which of these carbocations is tertiary?

choices.text: (CH3)2C+CH2CH3
(CH3)2CHCH2+
choices.why: The positive carbon is a CH2 with only one alkyl group: a primary carbocation.

choices.text: CH3CH2CH+CH3
choices.why: The positive carbon carries two alkyl groups (methyl and ethyl): a secondary carbocation.

choices.text: CH3+
choices.why: This is the methyl carbocation, with no alkyl groups.

explanation: In (CH3)2C+CH2CH3 the positive carbon is bonded to three alkyl groups, two methyls and an ethyl, so it is tertiary, the most stable type.

prompt: 2-Methylpropene could add H+ to form either a tertiary or a primary carbocation. What observation shows that the tertiary cation is favored?

choices.text: The tertiary alkyl chloride, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, is the only product observed with HCl
The primary alkyl chloride, 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, is the major product with HCl
choices.why: 1-Chloro-2-methylpropane isn't formed at all; only the tertiary chloride is observed.

choices.text: Equal amounts of the tertiary and primary alkyl chlorides are formed with HCl
choices.why: No mixture is observed; the tertiary chloride is the sole product.

choices.text: No alkyl chloride forms, because the carbocation can't react with Cl−
choices.why: The carbocation does react with Cl−, giving 2-chloro-2-methylpropane as the only product.

explanation: Since the tertiary alkyl chloride, 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, is the only product observed, formation of the tertiary cation is evidently favored over the primary one. Thermodynamic measurements confirm that more substituted carbocations are more stable.

prompt: Which measurement does the book use to compare carbocation stabilities?

choices.text: The energy needed to form each cation from its alkyl halide, R–X → R^+ + X^−
The heat released when the alkene that gives each cation is hydrogenated
choices.why: Heats of hydrogenation compare alkene stabilities (Section 7.6), not carbocation stabilities.

choices.text: The rate at which each carbocation is captured by a bromide ion
choices.why: The book compares carbocations by the energy needed to form them from alkyl halides, not by how fast they react.

choices.text: The number of hydrogens counted on each positively charged carbon
choices.why: Counting groups classifies a carbocation, but its stability is measured by the energy needed to form it from an alkyl halide.

explanation: One way to determine carbocation stabilities is to measure the amount of energy required to form a carbocation by dissociation of the corresponding alkyl halide, R–X → R^+ + :X^−. Tertiary alkyl halides dissociate more easily than secondary or primary ones.

prompt: Which alkyl chloride dissociates most easily into a carbocation and Cl− in the gas phase?

choices.text: t-Butyl chloride, (CH3)3CCl
Chloromethane, CH3Cl
choices.why: Chloromethane needs the most energy (about 940 kJ/mol), since it gives the least stable methyl cation.

choices.text: Chloroethane, CH3CH2Cl
choices.why: Chloroethane gives a primary cation and needs about 810 kJ/mol.

choices.text: Isopropyl chloride, (CH3)2CHCl
choices.why: Isopropyl chloride gives a secondary cation (about 710 kJ/mol); t-butyl chloride gives a tertiary one more easily (about 680 kJ/mol).

explanation: Figure 7.9.2 shows that more highly substituted alkyl halides dissociate more easily: about 940 kJ/mol for chloromethane, 810 for chloroethane, 710 for isopropyl chloride, and 680 for t-butyl chloride, which forms the tertiary carbocation.

prompt: Figure 7.9.2 gives gas-phase dissociation enthalpies of about 940 kJ/mol for chloromethane and 680 kJ/mol for t-butyl chloride. How much less energy, in kJ/mol, does t-butyl chloride need?
explanation: 940 − 680 = 260 kJ/mol. The tertiary carbocation is much easier to form than the methyl cation, reflecting its greater stability.

prompt: How do the dissociation enthalpies for forming carbocations in solution compare with those in the gas phase?

choices.text: Much lower, since polar solvents stabilize the ions, but in the same order
Much higher, since the ions must push solvent molecules aside
choices.why: They are much lower, since polar solvents stabilize the ions.

choices.text: Much lower, and the order of carbocation stability is reversed
choices.why: The dissociation enthalpies drop, but the order of carbocation stability remains the same.

choices.text: About the same, since solvents don't interact with the ions
choices.why: Polar solvents stabilize ions, so dissociation enthalpies are much lower in solution.

explanation: The data in Figure 7.9.2 come from gas-phase measurements. In solution the dissociation enthalpies are much lower because polar solvents can stabilize the ions, but the order of carbocation stability remains the same.

prompt: What two effects explain why more highly substituted carbocations are more stable?

choices.text: Inductive effects and hyperconjugation
Steric strain and hyperconjugation
choices.why: Steric strain is destabilizing, and it isn't one of the reasons given. The two are inductive effects and hyperconjugation.

choices.text: Inductive effects and stronger sp3–sp2 bonds
choices.why: Bond strength was a factor in alkene stability (Section 7.6). For carbocations, the reasons are inductive effects and hyperconjugation.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding and inductive effects
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding isn't involved. The second factor is hyperconjugation.

explanation: There are at least two reasons: inductive effects, in which electrons from alkyl groups shift toward the positive charge, and hyperconjugation, the interaction of the vacant p orbital with neighboring C–H σ bonds.

prompt: How do inductive effects make a tertiary carbocation more stable than a primary one?

choices.text: Alkyl groups shift electron density toward the positive charge more easily than H
Alkyl groups pull electron density away from the positive carbon more than H
choices.why: It's the reverse: electron density shifts toward the positive charge, making the carbon less electron-poor.

choices.text: Hydrogens shift electron density toward the positive charge more easily than alkyl groups
choices.why: Alkyl groups, being larger and more polarizable, shift electrons more easily than hydrogen does.

choices.text: Each alkyl group donates a lone pair into the vacant p orbital
choices.why: Alkyl groups have no lone pairs. The effect is a shift of σ-bond electrons toward the charge.

explanation: Inductive effects result from the shifting of electrons in a σ bond. Electrons from a relatively larger and more polarizable alkyl group shift toward a neighboring positive charge more easily than the electron from a hydrogen, so the more alkyl groups attached, the more inductive stabilization (Figure 7.9.3).

prompt: What is hyperconjugation in a carbocation?

choices.text: Overlap of the vacant p orbital with roughly parallel C–H σ bonds on neighboring carbons
Overlap of the vacant p orbital with C–H σ bonds on the positive carbon itself
choices.why: The C–H bonds involved are on the neighboring carbons, not on the cationic carbon.

choices.text: Overlap of the vacant p orbital with neighboring C–H σ bonds perpendicular to it
choices.why: Only C–H bonds roughly parallel to the p orbital are oriented properly; a perpendicular one can't take part.

choices.text: Repulsion between the alkyl groups crowded around the positive carbon
choices.why: Hyperconjugation is a stabilizing interaction involving C–H σ bonds and the empty p orbital.

explanation: Hyperconjugation is the stabilizing interaction between a p orbital and properly oriented C–H σ bonds on neighboring carbons that are roughly parallel to the p orbital. The more alkyl groups on the carbocation, the more possibilities for hyperconjugation.

prompt: In the ethyl carbocation, CH3CH2+, as pictured in Figure 7.9.4, how many of the methyl group's C–H bonds are oriented properly (roughly parallel to the vacant p orbital) to take part in hyperconjugation?
explanation: Of the three C–H bonds on the methyl group, the two more parallel to the cation's p orbital are oriented properly for hyperconjugation; the one perpendicular to the p orbital can't take part properly.

prompt: How many alkyl groups are bonded to the positively charged carbon of a secondary carbocation?
explanation: Carbocations are classified by the number of alkyl substituents on the positive carbon: one for primary, two for secondary, three for tertiary, and none for the methyl cation, CH3+.

prompt: Which carbocation intermediate would you expect when 2,4-dimethyl-3-hexene, (CH3)2CHCH=C(CH3)CH2CH3, reacts with HBr?

choices.text: A tertiary carbocation at C4, formed by adding H+ to C3
A secondary carbocation at C3, formed by adding H+ to C4
choices.why: C3 has only two alkyl groups. Adding H+ to C3 instead puts the charge on C4, which has three.

choices.text: A tertiary carbocation at C2, formed by adding H+ to C3
choices.why: H+ adds to one double-bond carbon and the charge appears on the other. C2 isn't part of the double bond.

choices.text: A secondary carbocation at C4, formed by adding H+ to C3
choices.why: With H+ on C3, the positive C4 carries three alkyl groups (a methyl, an ethyl, and C3), so it is tertiary.

explanation: C3 carries one hydrogen and C4 carries none. Adding H+ to C3 puts the positive charge on C4, which is bonded to three alkyl groups, so the more stable tertiary cation forms (Exercise 7.9.1).

prompt: Ethylidenecyclopentane is a cyclopentane ring whose ring carbon is double-bonded to a CHCH3 group. Which carbocation intermediate would you expect when it reacts with HI?

choices.text: A tertiary carbocation on the ring carbon, formed by adding H+ to the CHCH3 carbon
A secondary carbocation on the side-chain carbon, formed by adding H+ to the ring carbon
choices.why: That cation has only two alkyl groups. Putting H+ on the side-chain carbon leaves the charge on the ring carbon, which has three.

choices.text: A primary carbocation on the CH3 carbon, formed by adding H+ to the CHCH3 carbon
choices.why: The CH3 carbon isn't part of the double bond, so the charge can't appear there by adding H+.

choices.text: A tertiary carbocation on a ring carbon next to the double bond
choices.why: The charge appears on one of the two double-bond carbons, not on a neighboring ring carbon.

explanation: The ring carbon of the double bond is bonded to two ring carbons, and the side-chain carbon is bonded to one CH3. Adding H+ to the side-chain carbon leaves the positive charge on the ring carbon, giving a tertiary cation: ethylcyclopentane with the charge on C1 (Exercise 7.9.1).
